At 1 atm, a liquid with 95 mol% ethanol is in equilibrium with a vapour of about **94.7 mol% ethanol and 5.3 mol% water**. The boiling (bubble) point is about **78.2 °C**.

The vapour has slightly less ethanol than the liquid. That is because this liquid is past the ethanol–water azeotrope, which sits near 89–90 mol% ethanol at 1 atm. Above that point ethanol is the less volatile component, so ordinary distillation at 1 atm can't purify a 95% liquid any further. The vapour is pushed back toward the azeotrope.

I computed this rather than recalling it. The method was modified Raoult's law (gas phase treated as ideal) with Antoine vapour pressures, which reproduce the pure boiling points of 78.32 °C and 100.00 °C. I checked it with two activity-coefficient models:

| Model | T at x = 0.95 | y ethanol | Predicted azeotrope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wilson (Λ12 = 0.1782, Λ21 = 0.8681) | 78.19 °C | 0.9467 | x ≈ 0.90, 78.15 °C |
| Van Laar (A12 = 1.6798, A21 = 0.9227) | 78.24 °C | 0.9481 | x ≈ 0.89–0.90, 78.22 °C |

The two models agree to about 0.0015 in y. Both place the azeotrope close to the commonly quoted value of 89.4 mol% ethanol at 78.15 °C.

Limitations:
- I recalled the model parameters from memory and did not check them against a primary data source. Their main support is that both sets reproduce the known azeotrope.
- I did not compare against measured VLE data at x = 0.95. Expect an uncertainty of roughly ±0.005 in y.
- A first attempt with recalled NRTL parameters predicted no azeotrope at all. The parameters were evidently wrong, so I discarded that result.
